## DEFECT 1, migration mis-attributes wear — FIXED (`app/js/store.js`, `migrateWearMap`)

**Reproduced** through the real `importCharacter`: two Anvil Frames (`eq_a1`, `eq_a2`) with `eq_a2` WORN, legacy `armorWear:{"Anvil Frame":3}`, `armorGuard:{"Anvil Frame":true}`, plus two Scrap Shields with `eq_s2` wielded and `shieldWear:{"Scrap Shield":2}`. Migrated to `{eq_a1:3}` / `{eq_a1:true}` / `{eq_s1:2}`. The worn suit read **5/5**, `d.armorDR` **5**; the spare in the Stash read **2/5** and held the quality edge; the wielded shield read a full 2/2 while the spare took the destruction.

**Diagnosis, not symptom.** The rule was "a name becomes that item's FIRST owned entry". The first owned entry is not the damaged one, and the record already knows which one was: on `main` the reader is `(ch.shieldWear||{})[shield.name]` with `shield` the *wielded* shield, and the only writer `markShieldWear` returns early unless a shield is wielded; armor DR was only ever read for `ch.equippedArmor`. A legacy name key can only ever have described the piece in the slot.

**The resolution rule now:** live entry key kept (idempotency) → else the **equipped piece** if it carries that name (attribution, not a tiebreak) → else the **single owned entry** of that name → else **dropped**. Invariant four intact and strengthened.

**After:** `{eq_a2:3}` / `{eq_a2:true}` / `{eq_s2:2}`; worn suit 2/5 with guard, spare untouched 5/5. Eight shapes, all byte-stable across three loads: the defect shape, two-of-a-kind-none-worn (drops to `{}`), one-owned-not-worn (kept), legacy id-less `qty:2` with a name-valued equip slot, unowned name (dropped), prototype keys/junk/non-object maps (`{}`, no throw), already-entry-keyed (untouched), wear 99 vs base 5 (reads 0/5).

## BLOCKING: the live-key fast path bypasses attribution entirely and relocates wear onto a different piece, and a different item

`app/js/store.js:563`

```js
if (wearLiveKeys[k]) key = k;                       // already an entry key: idempotent
```

`wearLiveKeys` is built at `app/js/store.js:536-542` from `var k = e.id || e.name`, so it holds **ids and names in one flat namespace**. The fast path asks only "is this string a live entry key", never "does the entry it names actually bear this item name". When an entry's `id` equals another entry's item `name`, a legacy name key is claimed by the id-holder and rules 1/2/3 never run. Invariant four is not reached, so the state is neither attributed nor dropped: it is moved.

Failing scenario, run through the real `EN.store.load()` and independently through the real `EN.store.importCharacter()`, identical result both ways:

```
equipment: [ {id:"Anvil Frame", name:"Bastion Plate", qty:1},
             {id:"eq_a2",       name:"Anvil Frame",   qty:1} ]
equippedArmor: "eq_a2"
armorWear:  {"Anvil Frame": 3}
armorGuard: {"Anvil Frame": true}
```

After one load, `EN.engine.ownedArmorPieces`:

```
Anvil Frame <Bastion Plate>  2/5  GUARD     <- never damaged, now carries the loss and the quality edge
eq_a2       <Anvil Frame>    5/5            <- the WORN suit that was actually damaged, reads full
```

`armorWear` stays `{"Anvil Frame":3}`, `armorGuard` `{"Anvil Frame":true}`. The rule the report states ("live entry key kept, else the equipped piece if it carries that name, else the single owned entry, else dropped") is not what the code does: the first clause fires on a key the equipped piece does not hold, and short-circuits the other three.

Three consequences, all reproduced:

- **Wrong-item damage.** Above. The worn suit silently un-damages, a spare takes the loss.
- **A never-damaged suit reads BREACHED and is offered the rebuild lane.** Same shape with the decoy being a Liner Mesh (`dr 1`): `Anvil Frame <Liner Mesh> 0/1 BREACHED` beside `eq_a2 <Anvil Frame> 5/5`. `armorState` clamps on the *decoy's* base, so a 3-point loss becomes a 0 DR piece. That is the 𝒢500 rebuild Project offered on a suit that was never hit. With `armorWear:{"Anvil Frame":9}` on a Riot Wall decoy the raw 9 is retained in the map and the piece renders `0/4 BREACHED`.
- **It moves a SECOND time on a later load, so it is not idempotent for this class.** Load 1 lands the wear on the Bastion Plate. The player then sells the Bastion Plate. Load 2: the key is no longer live, so rule 2 now fires and the wear plus the guard jump again, to `eq_a2` (`{"Anvil Frame":3,guard} -> {"eq_a2":3,"eq_a2":true}`, piece reads `eq_a2 <Anvil Frame> 2/5 G`). Damage migrating between pieces across ordinary loads with no user action on the wear is exactly the failure mode this branch exists to stop. Control case with a normal `eq_b1` id is stable across the same sell-and-reload.

`equippedEntryKey` at `app/js/store.js:548-553` has the identical root cause in its own first clause (`if (wearLiveKeys[slotVal]) return slotVal;`), so a slot value that is a bare name colliding with some entry's id would seed rule 1 with the wrong piece too.

**Root cause, not symptom:** the fast path treats "is a live key" as proof of identity, but `e.id || e.name` makes ids and names one namespace, so a string can be a live key for one entry and an item name for others simultaneously. The fix has to make that ambiguity re-enter the rules rather than skip them: a key that is live **and** also appears in `wearKeysByName` naming any entry other than itself is ambiguous, and must go through rule 1 / rule 2 / drop like any other name. Silent relocation is not an acceptable outcome for any input shape, and a hand-authored id is squarely inside the threat model the block immediately above already accepts (`app/js/store.js:353-360`, "That deliberately includes a hand-edited non-string id"). `importCharacter` runs `migrate` on arbitrary JSON and reproduces it.

**Reachability, stated honestly:** no in-app path mints an `id` that is an item name (`inventory.js` and `builder.js` both mint `eq_*`), and a pooled name-keyed entry cannot coexist with a tracked entry of the same name because `isStackableName` is a pure function of the name. So this needs an imported or hand-edited record. It is not reachable by clicking. It is reachable by the one operation whose whole job is to ingest foreign records, it produces silent unrecoverable corruption when it happens, and the report claims the rule holds unconditionally, which it does not.

## Non-blocking: the merge of a name key and an id key is decided by JSON key order

`app/js/store.js:573` — `if (!key || out[key] != null) return;`

With two Anvil Frames, `eq_a1` worn, a map carrying both a legacy name key and a live id key for the same piece:

- `{"Anvil Frame":3, "eq_a1":1}` -> `{eq_a1: 3}` (the stale name value wins, the live value is discarded)
- `{"eq_a1":1, "Anvil Frame":3}` -> `{eq_a1: 1}` (the live value wins)

Same piece either way, so this is a wrong number rather than a wrong suit, and it is well below the blocking bar. But the outcome depends on nothing but property order in the file, and the safer ordering is free: resolve every live entry key first, then let name keys fill only the entries still unclaimed. Related and equally minor: `armorWear` and `armorGuard` resolve independently, so a record with `armorWear:{"Anvil Frame":3}` and `armorGuard:{"eq_a2":true}` ends with the loss on the worn `eq_a1` and the repair edge on the spare `eq_a2`.

### FINDING 1 (severe, and a regression this branch introduced): the new refund is not idempotent, so `✓ COMPLETE` mints Glimmer without bound

`app/js/inventory.js:2212` `tbComplete(p)` — refund computed at `:2226`, applied at `:2239`, splice at `:2232`.

`tbComplete` takes the project OBJECT captured at render. It removes it by id inside `tbSetProjects` but never checks the project is still in the list, and the branch's new `refund` line reads `p.materialsPaid` off that still-live object. Every re-entry recomputes `restored` as 0 (the suit is already whole) and pays the refund again. `tbSecure` got exactly this guard at `:2196` (`if (p.materialsSecured) return;`) and `armorShopRepair` got the live re-read; `tbComplete` got neither.

Failing scenario, run live — Anvil Frame (𝒢920, DR 5), 3 lost, wallet 𝒢5000. `⚒ BENCH · 𝒢138` → `SECURE · 𝒢138` → three `Strong` intervals → one rendered `✓ COMPLETE` node fired four times:

```
4862  suit 2/5 -> 5/5      (correct)
5000  +138 "unused parts refunded"   suit already 5/5
5138  +138
5276  +138
```

Player started at 5000, bought a legitimate 3 DR repair, ended at 5276. Each further fire adds another 138. On the leased rebuild lane the unit is bigger: Sentinel Issue breached, `⚒ REBUILD PROJECT · 𝒢500`, secure, complete, complete → `2000 → 1500 → (suit 3/3) 1500 → 2000`. This is reachable by re-firing the handler, which is precisely the repro the implementer used to justify the `armorShopRepair` fix ("one rendered SHOP button fired three times: 1000 → 172"). ## What the lens confirmed as genuinely good

- **Defect 3, all three paths.** Sentinel Issue (deposit 150, `buyout: 1000`, DR 3), 2 lost, worn: `▤ SHOP · 𝒢200` / `⚒ BENCH · 𝒢100`; breached: `⚒ REBUILD PROJECT · 𝒢500`. Bailiff Rig (deposit 430, `nexus: "◎0.3 buyout"`, DR 5), 3 lost: `▤ SHOP · 𝒢900` / `⚒ BENCH · 𝒢450`; breached: `⚒ REBUILD PROJECT · 𝒢1,500`. Both buyout forms resolve, nothing prices off the deposit. Unleased Anvil Frame unchanged at 92/184/276/460. The rebuild's use of `rebuildCost` creates no arbitrage against Blueprints, because `tbBlueprints` (`inventory.js:2547`) filters `!it.upkeep` and leased items are not buildable at `materialCost` at all.
- **Defect 4, per point, in each lane, restoring exactly what was bought.** Anvil Frame 3 lost: picker steps `3/3 → 2/3 → 1/3` repricing `276/184/92` shop and `138/92/46` bench, and clamps at 1. - **The 10 percent rate still derives.** `shopCost(Anvil, 5) = 460`, exactly half the 𝒢920 list; `rebuildCost(Anvil) = 460`, the same half. Ratio intact.
- **Defect 5, the two paths that were named.** `✓ COMPLETE` is `disabled` while materials are owed, on repairs and on the leased rebuild alike, and `tbComplete` re-checks. Both zero-restore paths refund (piece left the Stash: `4862 → 5000`; suit repaired another way first: `4586 → 4724`). `tbSecure` cannot double-charge.

## Verdict on mergeability

Not as it stands. Finding 2 is a plain user-reachable debit with no restore inside the exact feature Defect 5 was raised about, and Finding 1 is a currency-creation hole introduced by the fix for that same defect, of the same class the branch fixed one function away. Both are one-line fixes: refund `materialsPaid` for `repairKey` projects in `tbAbandon` (and say so in the confirm), and give `tbComplete` the `tbSecure` guard by re-finding the project by id inside `tbSetProjects` and bailing when it is gone.
